entry.evidence: WT noise and earthquake signals have overlapping frequency bands, and thus spectral filtering cannot be used.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text) with PDF for figures

steps.action: Take from prior studies that wind-turbine noise degrades seismological station quality, which led to protection radii around stations.
steps.quote: All mentioned studies come to the conclusion that the data quality is deteriorating due to the expansion of WTs.

steps.action: Pose the question of how to suppress WT noise that shares the earthquake frequency band and can fully cover events, where spectral filtering and published CWT examples fall short.
steps.quote: Sometimes, the earthquake signal is completely covered by noise and therefore not visible in either the time or the time-frequency domain.

steps.action: Adopt two published denoising methods as candidates: nonlinear thresholding of CWT coefficients (Langston and Mousavi) and the convolutional denoising autoencoder (Zhu et al., Tibi et al.).
steps.quote: [...] . (37), Mandelli et al. (18), and Tibi et al. (30) have developed a new approach that uses a convolutional denoising autoencoder (DAE)

steps.action: Propose that a DAE using the CWT, with its different resolution, may suppress noise more accurately than the STFT used before.
steps.quote: so CWT may be able to suppress noise more accurately, which was not tested in previous studies.

steps.action: Compute hourly wind-speed-binned PSD curves for several NRW stations and find at RN.BAVN wind-dependent peaks at 3.2 and 4.2 Hz and a 20 dB deterioration from 2012 to 2019.
steps.quote: The comparison of the yellow PSD curves (Fig. 1) shows a deterioration of 20 dB between 2012 and 2019

steps.action: Check against stations with fewer or no turbines, which show no similar wind dependence.
steps.quote: PSD curves at other stations where fewer or no WT were installed do not show similar wind dependencies.

steps.action: Select the affected station RN.BAVN, near six turbines built 2009-2017, as the study site.
steps.quote: [...] , we selected the seismological station RN.BAVN for our study.

steps.action: Install short-period seismometers 50-80 m from each turbine and obtain turbine operation parameters, to record the noise at its source.
steps.quote: we installed short period seismometers (Raspberry Shakes RS3D and Mark L-4C3D) close to each WT (50 to 80 m away from the foundation).

steps.action: Implement the Morlet CWT (Torrence and Compo) with soft thresholding and a scale-dependent threshold set as the 0.99 quantile of a noise estimate.
steps.quote: Alternatively, thresholding can also be done by shrinking all coefficients that exceed the threshold function.

steps.action: Hypothesise that noise similarity between time windows at the turbines carries over to the station, so a past station window can serve as a noise model.
steps.quote: if the noise recorded close to a WT in the event window and a different time window are very similar, this also holds

steps.action: Design the similarity search: normalised Euclidean distance between the pre-event master window at each turbine sensor and earlier windows of equal length.
steps.quote: To check this hypothesis, we took records form the sensors close to the WTs and calculated the Euclidean distance

steps.action: Test the distance profile on a synthetic time series with hidden copies of the master signal at different amplitudes; local minima recover their locations.
steps.quote: The resulting distance profile is zero (global minimum) at the timestamp of the master signal and has local minima at the timestamps of similar signals.

steps.action: Average the distance profiles over turbines, take the second-smallest minimum, and extract a 60 s station waveform at that time as the noise model for the threshold.
steps.quote: The final step is to extract the waveform at the seismological station at the time of the minimum in the average distance profile

steps.action: Build a modified mask-based DAE (dropout, skip connections, CWT or STFT input) and train it on 100,000 high-SNR STEAD earthquakes mixed with more than 100,000 RN.BAVN noise windows.
steps.quote: we add dropout to each convolutional layer to prevent the neural network from overfitting

steps.action: Test both DAEs on 5000 held-out noisy waveforms with known clean signals; mean SNR rises from 6.0 to 26.6 dB but does not reach the original 42.8 dB.
steps.quote: To evaluate the performance of the trained network, we create a test dataset from events and noise signals, which were not used for training.

steps.action: Compare CWT and STFT DAEs on the test set: equal mean gain, slightly wider distribution and more events at 35-45 dB for CWT.
steps.quote: Comparing the denoised histograms, CWT achieves a slightly better result than STFT

steps.action: Apply both DAEs to 2421 real M>1 events recorded at RN.BAVN in 2017-2020, with arrivals estimated from surrounding stations; mean SNR rises by about 4.4 dB, and many low-SNR events stay low.
steps.quote: The histograms show clearly that many events with low SNR retained a low SNR after denoising.

steps.action: Compare raw data, a 5-20 Hz bandpass, thresholding with pre-noise, thresholding with the noise model, and both DAEs on four selected events of decreasing SNR.
steps.quote: We compared the performance of the DAE with both nonlinear thresholding and a bandpass filter between 5 and 20 Hz

steps.action: Exclude bandpass filtering and both thresholding variants for an event fully covered by noise, where only the DAEs make the event visible.
steps.quote: Nonlinear thresholding also fails (Fig. 15(III) and (IV)), no matter which method is used.

steps.action: Apply the DAEs to a three-component seismogram; results hold on the horizontal components and the S-phase can be picked.
steps.quote: The denoising results do not differ significantly when the horizontal components are included

steps.action: Reject the turbine-based noise model in favour of pre-noise, which suppresses noise better, needs no extra sensors, and runs almost in real time.
steps.quote: Using pre-noise is therefore superior (to the noise-model determination) as it can almost be done in real time.

steps.action: Refine the CWT hypothesis: CWT is at best slightly better than STFT, at a much higher training cost.
steps.quote: In conclusion, there is no big difference when using CWT or STFT as time-frequency transformation.

steps.action: Keep the DAE as the only tested method that separates WT noise from signal in a shared frequency band, with the limits of the mask approach noted.
steps.quote: The DAE is the only one of the methods investigated that is capable of separating noise and signal well

steps.action: Run the DAE in real time on overlapping 60 s windows merged with ObsPy; no quantitative result is reported.
steps.quote: We also tested the DAE on real time denoising.

tree.answer: WT noise degrades station quality in the 1-10 Hz band (cited; confirmed at RN.BAVN)
Yes: wind-binned PSD curves show a 20 dB increase and wind-dependent peaks
Suppress WT noise; compare denoising techniques
Bandpass filter, thresholding with pre-noise, thresholding with a turbine-derived noise model, DAE with CWT, DAE with STFT
Only that CWT might outperform STFT; no explicit predictions for the other methods
Found: an affected station selected; test mixtures constructed from held-out data
DAE gain holds on held-out mixtures, 2421 real events and three components, though smaller on real data
DAE kept as best; noise model and thresholding fail for buried events; CWT not clearly better

end.claim: A DAE trained on station noise and high-SNR earthquakes suppresses wind-turbine noise even when the event is fully covered, whereas thresholding works only when the event is already visible; mean real-data SNR gain is about 4.4 dB.

decisive_move.sentence: The head-to-head comparison of bandpass, both thresholding variants and both DAEs on real events at the affected station is what ranks the DAE above the rivals.

gates.evidence: Action: the noise-transfer hypothesis (§3.1 ¶2) motivates using the turbine sensors, but the Fig. 2 caption says the sensors were installed 'for the development and testing of a denoising algorithm', so it is unclear whether the hypothesis preceded the installation. Claim: the DAE faced held-out and real-data SNR tests it could have failed (§4.1). The method ranking rests on four selected events (§4.2), and the full real dataset was run through the DAE only. Registration: no threshold, metric or test plan is stated as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Convolutional denoising autoencoder with dropout, batch normalisation, softmax masks and Adam optimiser
Skip connections in denoising auto-encoders for source separation (Liu and Yang)
Wavelet-shrinkage nonlinear thresholding (Donoho and Johnstone; Donoho)
Soft thresholding with wavelet transforms (Weaver et al.)
Matrix-profile normalised Euclidean distance similarity search (Yeh et al.; Zhu et al. 2016)

novelty_claims.quote: so CWT may be able to suppress noise more accurately, which was not tested in previous studies.

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The method comparison against bandpass and thresholding uses four selected events (§4.2), with no stated selection rule. Inference: the examples may favour visible contrasts. Thresholding was not run on the 2421-event dataset, so the ranking of rivals is not quantified at scale. The noise-transfer hypothesis (§3.1 ¶2) is never tested directly. Only a worked example is given (Fig. 6), and the noise model is rejected on performance, not because the transfer was shown false. Real-data SNR uses arrivals estimated from other stations, an untested auxiliary. The real-time test (§5 ¶7) reports no result. The DAE's failure limits are stated as unknown (§5 ¶3). The no-time-shift, no-polarity-change claim (§5 ¶5) rests on visual inspection of Figs. 16-17 and is not coded as a V check. Sub-claims and statuses: thresholding with pre-noise works when the event is visible (capability_characterized, consistent with Mousavi et al. and Langston and Mousavi); the turbine-based noise model does not improve on pre-noise (rival excluded, on four examples); CWT versus STFT shows no big difference, with CWT slightly better (best_explanation, weak); DAE applicable to three components (capability_characterized, one example). Composition is none_fits because the walk is a benchmark comparison of candidate methods on found data, not a trace series, a strong-inference test, or capability-first exploration.

disagreements.target: Mousavi et al. (2016); Langston and Mousavi (2019), CWT thresholding
disagreements.support: The paper shows thresholding works only when the event is visible and fails when the event is fully covered by WT noise (Figs. 14-15).
disagreements.quote: the signal is always visible in the noisy raw data in the examples shown, which is not always true [...] .

disagreements.target: Zhu et al. (2019); Tibi et al. (2021), STFT-only DAE
disagreements.support: The paper tests a CWT-input DAE against an STFT-input DAE and finds only a slight advantage for CWT at higher cost, which largely supports the STFT choice.
disagreements.quote: Zhu et al. (37) and Tibi et al. (30) only used the STFT which has a lower time-frequency resolution than [...] .

disagreements.target: Protection radii of 5-15 km around stations (Stammler and Ceranna 2016; Bavarian and NRW wind-energy decrees)
disagreements.support: The paper frames denoising as a way to limit land loss from protection radii. Inference: it does not explicitly argue for smaller radii.
disagreements.quote: Due to the large protection radii, a lot of potential area is lost that could be used for wind energy.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both CWT and STFT as DAE input, compared
alternatives_considered.alternatives: STFT only, as in Zhu et al. and Tibi et al.
alternatives_considered.reason: STFT and CWT have different resolutions; CWT untested
STFT is limited in time-frequency resolution
Hard thresholding results in lower SNR if noise outliers are above the threshold

alternatives_considered.chosen: Pre-noise window for the threshold function
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Noise model extracted via turbine similarity search
alternatives_considered.reason: Pre-noise suppresses noise better, is simpler and can run almost in real time

alternatives_considered.chosen: Normalised Euclidean distance for similarity search
alternatives_considered.reason: Computationally more efficient for large datasets

alternatives_considered.chosen: CWT input downsampled by a factor of 2
alternatives_considered.reason: Otherwise the input layer would be too large for the memory

alternatives_considered.chosen: Two mask functions for signal and noise
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Real and imaginary output layers for the signal
alternatives_considered.reason: none given (alternative proposed as future improvement)
